Associated injuries are treated in the same plan: cribriform leaks, the frontal outflow tract, and the lacrimal system (late DCR).

imaging.ct: Thin-section axial and coronal CT: fracture and displacement of the medial orbital rim and frontal process of the maxilla (the central fragment), nasal bones telescoped into the ethmoid, widened intercanthal distance, comminuted lamina papyracea and lacrimal fossa, and disruption of the nasolacrimal canal. Check the cribriform plate and anterior skull base (pneumocephalus, CSF leak), the frontal sinus floor and outflow tract, and the other orbital walls.

redFlags: Telecanthus or a rounded, displaced medial canthus → central fragment or tendon displacement; repair early.
Clear rhinorrhea → cribriform or ethmoid roof fracture ([[dz.csf-leak-traumatic]]).
Epiphora later → nasolacrimal obstruction ([[p.endoscopic-dcr]]).
Visual loss → traumatic optic neuropathy or retrobulbar hematoma.

conditions.name: Orbital floor (blowout) fracture
conditions.what: Fracture of the thin orbital floor, usually medial to the infraorbital canal and sometimes with the medial wall, from blunt orbital trauma. Orbital fat or the inferior rectus may herniate into the maxillary sinus, causing diplopia, enophthalmos and infraorbital numbness.
conditions.why: Muscle entrapment — typically a trapdoor fracture in a child — is repaired within hours to save the muscle; otherwise large defects, early enophthalmos or persisting diplopia are repaired electively through transconjunctival or endoscopic transantral routes. The endoscope through an antrostomy shows the posterior ledge on which an implant must rest, and loss of the inferomedial strut makes the implant harder to support.

imaging.ct: Thin-section coronal and sagittal CT: size and posterior extent of the floor defect (to the posterior ledge), herniated fat and inferior rectus in the antrum, a rounded or sagging inferior rectus belly (loss of support), antral hemosinus, orbital emphysema, and medial wall and inferomedial strut involvement. In a child's trapdoor fracture the floor can look almost normal, with only a small sliver of trapped soft tissue — the examination decides.

redFlags: Child with restricted up-gaze, pain on eye movement, nausea, vomiting or bradycardia (oculocardiac reflex) and a quiet white eye → trapdoor entrapment; repair urgently.
Visual loss or a tense, proptotic orbit → retrobulbar hematoma; lateral canthotomy and cantholysis.
Globe injury must be excluded by ophthalmology before repair.

conditions.name: Traumatic optic neuropathy
conditions.what: Visual loss after head or facial trauma from injury to the optic nerve — usually indirect, from force transmitted to the intracanalicular segment where the nerve is tethered, less often direct, from bone fragments or penetration. It is diagnosed by reduced acuity or field with a relative afferent pupillary defect.
conditions.why: Neither high-dose steroids nor canal decompression has proven benefit over observation (International Optic Nerve Trauma Study), and megadose steroids increased mortality after significant head injury (CRASH), so decompression ([[p.optic-nerve-decompression]]) is reserved for selected cases such as a fragment impinging on the nerve or delayed deterioration. If decompressing, confirm on CT whether the canal runs in an Onodi cell ([[c.delano-optic-nerve]]).

imaging.ct: Thin-section CT through the optic canals in axial and coronal planes: canal fracture, bone fragments impinging on the nerve, fractures of the anterior clinoid and lateral sphenoid wall, sphenoid hemosinus; in indirect injury the CT is often normal. Also look for retrobulbar hematoma and orbital apex fractures.
imaging.mri: May show optic nerve sheath hematoma or nerve signal change; rarely changes acute management.

redFlags: Visual loss with a tense, proptotic orbit → retrobulbar hematoma: lateral canthotomy and cantholysis first, not canal decompression.
RAPD in an unconscious trauma patient → document early; it may be the only sign.
Canal fracture with a fragment in the nerve and worsening vision → consider decompression.

conditions.name: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (sinonasal disease)
conditions.what: An ANCA-associated small- and medium-vessel vasculitis with eosinophil-rich tissue inflammation in which the nose and sinuses are among the most commonly involved organs. The sinonasal picture usually looks like chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, and it can precede recognition of the systemic vasculitis by several years.
conditions.why: Treat new polyposis as a possible marker of a systemic disease rather than as isolated CRS with polyps: in a scoping review the sinonasal presentation was clinically indistinguishable from CRS with polyps without EGPA, and the median time from CRS onset to EGPA diagnosis was 66 months (35 patients with data). A sinus biopsy rarely proves vasculitis (head and neck biopsies in 7 patients in one series showed none), so the diagnosis rests on the clinical and laboratory picture, and a negative biopsy does not exclude it. Destructive sinonasal disease points to GPA rather than EGPA ([[dz.gpa]]). Off-label dupilumab has been used mainly for disabling ENT symptoms, but EGPA flares occurred in about a third of 51 patients, so the authors advise caution.

imaging.ct: Nasal polyps with sinus disease are the usual picture (CRS with polyps was the predominant sinonasal phenotype in a scoping review). Compared with GPA on sinus CT (22 EGPA, 31 GPA), EGPA showed more high-density opacification and higher mean attenuation of secretions (both P < .0001), as in allergic fungal sinusitis, whereas bony destruction, sclerotic wall change and involvement of adjacent organs were more frequent in GPA. By Lund-Mackay score (30 EGPA patients before treatment) disease was on average milder than in NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease or eosinophilic CRS without asthma, with wide variation between patients: low scorers had only minor maxillary and anterior ethmoid findings, high scorers high ostiomeatal complex scores.

redFlags: Nasal polyps with obstructive airway disease and a blood eosinophil count at or above 1 x 10^9/L, or mononeuritis multiplex or motor neuropathy → think EGPA and involve rheumatology (these are items of the 2022 classification criteria, [[c.acr-eular-egpa]]).
Septal perforation, saddle nose or bony destruction → GPA is more likely: in one cross-sectional series (15 EGPA, 35 GPA) destructive lesions including saddle nose occurred only in GPA.
Negative sinus biopsy → does not exclude EGPA: biopsies in 7 patients in one series showed no vasculitis.
EGPA flare after starting dupilumab → in a 51-patient retrospective study, relapse on dupilumab was associated with blood eosinophilia in 14 of 16 patients.

pearls.text: In a Spanish single-centre series, sinonasal involvement was the most frequent head and neck manifestation (82% of 22 patients meeting the 2022 criteria; 21 had head and neck data), and nasal polyps were the commonest finding (7 of 21). Polyps were not significantly associated with ANCA positivity or eosinophilia.

In an older series of 28 patients with Churg-Strauss syndrome (1990 ACR criteria), 21 had ENT involvement; of those 21, nasal polyposis was present in 16, allergic rhinitis in 9 and nasal crusting in 3.

Across 109 studies in a scoping review (1,087 patients with CRS and EGPA), nasal polyps were present in 753 (69.3%) and absent in 334 (30.7%); because the studies used different criteria and populations, treat the split as indicative, not as a prevalence.

conditions.name: Primary ciliary dyskinesia (sinonasal disease)
conditions.what: A rare inherited disorder of motile cilia that impairs mucociliary clearance and causes chronic sinopulmonary disease. In the nose it causes chronic nasal symptoms and chronic rhinosinusitis, in sinuses that are often underdeveloped.
conditions.why: Read the CT for development before planning surgery: the frontal and sphenoid sinuses are frequently aplastic or hypoplastic, and marked turbinate hypertrophy and septal deviation are common, so check what is actually present before choosing the operation. Evidence for sinus surgery here is limited to very small series: in one series of four adults, symptom, quality-of-life and endoscopic scores improved at 3 and 6 months while olfaction did not. Sinonasal disease needs regular examination at every age, because in a 384-participant international cohort the only characteristic associated with more sinonasal disease was age 10 years or older.

imaging.ct: Adults (21 patients, Plantier): aplasia in 38.1% of frontal and 14.3% of sphenoid sinuses and hypoplasia in 47.6% of frontal, 54.8% of sphenoid and 40.5% of maxillary sinuses (percentages are per sinus); trabecular loss in 61.9% of ethmoid sinuses; mean Lund-Mackay score 13.5; marked bilateral inferior turbinate hypertrophy in 47.6%, marked middle turbinate hypertrophy in 38.1% and marked septal deviation in 47.6% (per patient). Images suggesting fungus ball, mucocele, osteoma, a possible antrochoanal polyp and frontal bone erosion were also found. In 17 patients with CT volumes (Pappa), maxillary, sphenoid and frontal sinus volumes were all significantly smaller than in matched controls.

redFlags: Frontal and/or sphenoid aplasia or hypoplasia on CT → may be part of the PCD spectrum and should prompt exclusion of PCD: in 86 patients evaluated for PCD, it was present in 30 of 41 with PCD (73%) against 17 of 45 (38%) with secondary ciliary dyskinesia.
Planning CT in PCD → expect incidental findings (fungus ball, mucocele, osteoma, frontal bone erosion were each reported in 21 adults) and absent or small sinuses.

pearls.text: In 384 participants (median age 16 years) of an international ENT cohort, chronic nasal problems were reported by 89%, nasal polyps found in 51 of 345 examined (15%), hypertrophic inferior turbinates in 127 of 341 (37%) and facial pain in 50 of 342 (15%); polyps, hypertrophic turbinates, deviated septum and facial pain were more common in adults, and hyposmia was reported by 24% of adults against 4% of children.

A single-centre comparison found PCD-related CRS had a more significant effect on sinonasal quality of life than CRS without nasal polyps and than cystic fibrosis, although PCD and CF share a mucociliary clearance defect (abstract only; no scores quoted here). See [[dz.cystic-fibrosis-sinusitis]].

conditions.name: Chronic rhinosinusitis with primary immunodeficiency (antibody deficiency)
conditions.what: Chronic or recurrent rhinosinusitis that is sustained by an immune defect, most often a primary antibody deficiency: common variable immunodeficiency (CVID), selective IgA deficiency, IgG subclass deficiency or specific antibody deficiency. It looks like ordinary CRS and is found by testing: in a prospective cohort of 138 adults with CRS no clinical characteristic predicted it. The sources read are about antibody deficiency and do not split the entity by immunodeficiency type; CF and ciliary disorders are separate causes of impaired clearance ([[dz.cystic-fibrosis-sinusitis]], [[dz.primary-ciliary-dyskinesia]]).
conditions.why: Check quantitative serum immunoglobulins and functional antibody responses in recalcitrant CRS before repeating surgery and before starting biologic therapy. Reported prevalence depends on the population: primary antibody deficiency was found in up to 50% of patients with recalcitrant CRS in the evidence-based review, but in an unselected adult CRS clinic cohort 21% (29 of 138) had hypogammaglobulinemia and only four had a clinically diagnosed deficiency. Treatment is shared with clinical immunology; immunoglobulin replacement appears most effective at high dose early in the disease, and surgery in this group is less clearly supported than replacement, though it may help if done early.

imaging.ct: No CT pattern that identifies the immunodeficiency itself was found in the sources read. In 19 CVID patients, Lund-Mackay mucosal thickening was inversely related to serum IgM (R = -0.6398, p = 0.0032) and osteitis of the sinus bone was almost exclusively found in patients with IgM below 25 mg/dl (p = 0.0074).

redFlags: Recalcitrant or recurrent CRS despite medical and surgical treatment → serum immunoglobulins and functional antibody responses (systematic review and review of primary antibody deficiencies in CRS both advise screening).
Before biologic therapy for CRS → immunoglobulin testing, because primary antibody deficiency is under-recognized and treatable (the authors of a 138-patient cohort).
Recurrent infections on immunoglobulin replacement → replacement does not remove them all: of 58 adults on replacement, 24 (41.4%) still reported 1 to 5 sinus infections a year.

pearls.text: Retrospective, uncontrolled data from 58 adults with primary humoral immunodeficiency and rhinosinusitis (30 CVID, 18 hypogammaglobulinemia, 10 specific antibody deficiency) on immunoglobulin replacement: mean Lund-Mackay score fell from 7.6 to 3.5, sinus surgery was needed before replacement in 11 (19%) and after it in 2 (3.4%), and 34 (58.6%) reported no further infections.

Among the antibody deficiencies reviewed, CRS is highly prevalent in CVID and selective IgA deficiency, the clinical relevance of IgG subclass deficiency is unclear, and specific antibody deficiency may matter more in refractory CRS.

conditions.name: Sinonasal tuberculosis
conditions.what: A rare mycobacterial granulomatous infection of the nose and paranasal sinuses, reported as primary disease in otherwise healthy, immunocompetent patients. Its signs and symptoms are non-specific and highly variable.
conditions.why: Keep it in the differential of nasal and paranasal sinus disease, particularly with intractable symptoms or a unilateral mass: primary sinonasal tuberculosis mimics sinonasal granulomatous disease and neoplasm. The diagnosis in the reported cases rested on imaging, nasal endoscopy and biopsy histology; tissue should be taken from several sites when the septum is ulcerated. In three reported cases antitubercular drug therapy was successful.

imaging.ct: No reliable CT sign is established by the abstracts read. A single reported case (Dey) showed a sinonasal mass involving the lateral nasal wall and the paranasal sinuses, and granulomatous diseases of the head and neck have imaging that overlaps with malignancy (Nwawka), so imaging cannot separate tuberculosis from neoplasm or other granulomatous disease.

redFlags: Septal ulceration or perforation → infective causes include tuberculosis and leprosy as well as vasculitis; diagnosis often needs multiple tissue specimens from several sites, and lymphoma should be considered in chronic cases (Sardana 2014).

A granulomatous biopsy of the nose is not automatically GPA or sarcoidosis → infectious causes (tuberculosis, syphilis, leprosy, rhinoscleroma, fungal) are listed alongside them in the head and neck granulomatous differential.

conditions.name: Leprosy of the nose (Hansen's disease, rhinomaxillary syndrome)
conditions.what: Chronic infection with Mycobacterium leprae in which lepromatous disease harbors large numbers of bacilli in the nasal tissue, often for years without symptoms. In advanced disease septal involvement leads to saddle nose deformity, and in long-standing disease CT shows resorption of the nasal bones, nasal aperture and anterior maxilla (rhinomaxillary syndrome).
conditions.why: Consider leprosy in a saddle nose or atrophic rhinitis that does not respond to routine treatment; in a reported case the diagnosis was made from acid-fast staining of the nasal discharge and a positive skin smear. CT is advised when rhinomaxillofacial bone change is suspected, and long-term care of former patients should include ENT evaluation, mainly to prevent secondary complications. Early diagnosis and treatment can minimize the damage.

imaging.ct: In a Brazilian study of 21 current and 16 former patients with 37 controls, severe resorption or atrophy of the anterior alveolar process of the maxilla was found in 8 of 16 former patients, 6 of 21 current patients and 4 of 37 controls, and of the nasal bones and aperture in 5 of 16 former patients, 0 of 21 current patients and two controls. In 16 older former patients examined by three-dimensional CT, 4 fully and 4 partly met radiological criteria for rhinomaxillary syndrome, and all with the full radiological syndrome had facial changes meeting the clinical criteria, including saddle nose and a concave middle third of the face. The criteria themselves were not read.

redFlags: Saddle nose or atrophic rhinitis that does not respond to routine treatment → acid-fast stain of nasal discharge and skin smear (one reported case, lepromatous leprosy).
Septal ulceration → leprosy and tuberculosis are among the infective causes; take multiple specimens (Sardana 2014).

conditions.name: Rhinoscleroma
conditions.what: A chronic, granulomatous infection of the upper airway caused by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis. The nose is involved in all cases, often with extension to the nasopharynx, larynx, trachea and bronchi. It is endemic in parts of Africa, South-East Asia, Mexico, Central and South America and Central and Eastern Europe, and is seen in other countries with migration.
conditions.why: Nasal symptoms are usually the first sign. Diagnosis rests on direct evidence of the bacterium (culture or immunohistochemistry on a nasal biopsy, with histology), and the differential diagnosis includes syphilis, midline granuloma and malignancy. Treatment is prolonged antibiotic therapy with reconstructive surgery when needed, but the disease is difficult to eradicate and recurs often. The paranasal sinuses are usually free of disease, so sinus or orbital extension is unusual and can mimic tumour or fungal sinusitis.

imaging.ct: CT and MRI are useful for diagnosis; the abstracts read describe no specific CT sign. The paranasal sinuses are usually free of disease (Bailhache).
imaging.mri: In a single reported case with orbital extension the lesion was homogeneously low signal on T2-weighted images and enhanced with gadolinium; it could simulate a malignant sinonasal tumour or a fungal sinusitis, so the diagnosis must be considered in patients from endemic areas.

redFlags: Chronic rhinitis or nasal granuloma in a patient from or with links to an endemic area → rhinoscleroma and ozena should be kept in mind even in developed countries, with biopsy for histology and bacterial identification.

conditions.name: Rhinosporidiosis
conditions.what: A chronic infection of the mucous membranes by Rhinosporidium seeberi, an aquatic mesomycetozoan, that primarily affects the nose (also the conjunctiva and urethra) and presents as a polypoid mass growing inside the affected cavity. It is endemic in some Asian regions and in parts of Brazil, and isolated cases are reported elsewhere with migration.
conditions.why: Keep it in mind for a polypoid, vascular-looking nasal or nasopharyngeal mass, including in patients from non-endemic countries. The only treatment is surgical excision, and the patient must be followed for recurrence. In a Brazilian series of 25 patients, most were children, adolescents or young adults, all lesions involved the entire nasal cavity as a vascular polypoid mass, and all were excised.

imaging.ct: The abstracts read describe no specific CT finding. In a reported case with proptosis from involvement of the nasolacrimal duct, the authors discuss typical CT and MRI features that the abstract does not state; they call CT and MRI invaluable, FNAC confirmatory, and rhinosporidiosis a necessary differential for sinonasal masses, which it may mimic as a more malignant lesion.

redFlags: Proptosis with a nasal mass → nasolacrimal duct involvement, a rare presentation reported in one case.

conditions.name: Nasal septal hematoma and abscess
conditions.what: Blood (hematoma) or pus (abscess) collecting between the septal cartilage and the overlying mucoperichondrium or mucoperiosteum. It follows nasal trauma or nasal surgery, and an untreated hematoma can become an abscess; abscess is typically secondary to a hematoma but can be idiopathic, and a spontaneous posterior septal abscess has been reported in a child. This entity covers the hematoma and the abscess together as one continuum; the surgical hazard of creating one is [[h.septal-hematoma]].
conditions.why: It is an emergency because delay destroys septal cartilage. Diagnosis is typically late (a mean 8.2 days from trauma in the meta-analysis of traumatic cases; a median 7 days in a paediatric series), and the reported sequelae are septal deformity or cartilage destruction (14.3% in the meta-analysis), saddle nose (3 of 13 children in one series) and, if an abscess is left, intracranial complications, facial deformity and delayed midface growth in children. Management is incision and drainage with antibiotics (in a management review of 17 articles and 503 patients incision and drainage was used in all, followed by quilting sutures, drains, nasal packing or a combination, and re-collection occurred in 18 patients, 3.6%); in children early septal reconstruction with autologous cartilage has been advised. After septoplasty, type 2 diabetes was an independent risk factor for abscess.

imaging.ct: The sources read describe CT only for the abscess: a fluid collection with thin rim enhancement within the cartilaginous septum, reported in two immunosuppressed patients (Debnam 2007). None of the sources read describes CT of the hematoma.

redFlags: Septal swelling and obstruction after nasal trauma or septal surgery → examine the septum and drain a collection; it is easily missed at first evaluation (a paediatric review found it missed in several settings before diagnosis).

Pain, fever or purulence with septal swelling → abscess: drainage, culture and antibiotics (Staphylococcus aureus was the commonest organism); intracranial abscess, meningitis and cavernous sinus thrombosis are the feared complications.

Picture of a septal abscess (nasal obstruction, headache, otalgia) with no recent trauma or infection and no anterior septal bulging → nasal endoscopy for a spontaneous posterior septal abscess (reported in a 10-year-old, confirmed on CT and MRI).

pearls.text: Meta-analysis of traumatic septal hematoma or abscess (30 studies, 598 patients; surgical cases excluded): 72.1% male, mean age 21.6 years; presenting symptoms nasal obstruction or congestion 60.3% (95% CI 37.1-81.4), nasal pain 30.0% (17.2-44.6), swelling 20.4% (8.7-35.5), headache 15.5% (7.3-26.0) and fever 13.9% (7.3-22.2); Staphylococcus aureus 56.5% (49.0-63.8) of isolated organisms.

In a Taiwanese insurance-database cohort (382 septoplasty patients with type 2 diabetes against 382 matched controls), the cumulative incidence of septal abscess after septoplasty was higher with diabetes (adjusted hazard ratio 2.62, 95% CI 1.44-3.61), and higher still with a Diabetes Complications Severity Index of 1 or more (adjusted hazard ratio 3.58, 2.10-6.09).

conditions.name: Nasolabial (nasoalveolar) cyst
conditions.what: A rare nonodontogenic cyst arising commonly in the nasal alar region, in the soft tissue between the nasolabial fold and the maxillary bone, usually presenting as facial swelling.
conditions.why: Two routes are used: intraoral sublabial excision, long the standard, and transnasal endoscopic marsupialization, an alternative that has emerged more recently. In a meta-analysis marsupialization had a shorter operative time, less postoperative pain, fewer complications, fewer admissions and lower costs, with no significant difference in recurrence; in the systematic review of 311 cases recurrence was reported in 3 patients after sublabial excision and 2 after marsupialization. The commonest complication after treatment was postoperative facial or perinasal swelling.

imaging.ct: CT was the most commonly used imaging in reported cases (170 of 311 patients in the systematic review). In 20 patients with 21 surgically proven cysts, all lay in the soft tissue between the nasolabial fold and the maxillary bone; for the diagnosis the sensitivity was 95% for ultrasound, 80% for CT and 85% for MRI (a small single-centre series).
imaging.mri: MRI had a sensitivity of 85% for nasolabial cysts in the same 20-patient series; the abstract does not describe signal characteristics.

pearls.text: In one 57-patient series (47 with preoperative CT), the mean operative time was 91.3 minutes for sublabial excision (23 patients) and 29.5 minutes for transnasal endoscopic marsupialization (34 patients), the hospitalization rate was 100% against 59%, and neither group had major complications or recurrence during 6 to 85 months of follow-up.
Laterality in reported cases where it was stated: left 46.9%, right 37.5%, bilateral 10.9% (systematic review of 311 cases).

conditions.name: Nasopalatine duct (incisive canal) cyst
conditions.what: The most common nonodontogenic cyst of the jaws, arising in the nasopalatine (incisive) canal and appearing as a well-defined radiolucency between the upper central incisors. In a 106-case series it behaved as a non-aggressive, slow-growing lesion, and most were asymptomatic in a systematic review (54.16% of cases).
conditions.why: Its position overlaps with odontogenic lesions of the upper incisors: a periapical cyst was the second most frequent clinical diagnostic hypothesis in a systematic review of 2,734 cases, and diagnosis needs radiographic and histopathological evaluation. Enucleation was the preferred treatment (544 cases, 95.94% of those with treatment reported) and recurrence was absent in most (375 cases, 93.05% of those with follow-up reported). Large cysts carry a risk of oronasal fistula; intranasal endoscopic marsupialization has been reported for them in a few cases and suggested as an initial option in selected cases.

imaging.ct: Midline location, smooth expansion with sclerotic margins and displacement of the tooth apices, in contrast to a radicular cyst in which the apices lie within the cyst (single reported case, Pevsner). On radiographs, a well-defined radiolucent lesion between the upper central incisors with a radiopaque margin (63-case series). On CBCT, the oral-opening mediolateral diameter, anterior wall expansion and mid-canal anteroposterior diameter were larger in 19 cysts than in 164 normal canals, and together they separated cysts from normal canals with a sensitivity of 98.8% and a specificity of 76.9%.

conditions.name: Organized hematoma of the maxillary sinus
syn: organizing hematoma of the maxillary sinus
conditions.what: A non-neoplastic, benign but sometimes locally aggressive mass of hemorrhage, fibrosis and neovascularization that arises most often in the maxillary sinus and extends into the ipsilateral nasal cavity. It presents with nasal bleeding, obstruction or facial swelling, and its pathogenesis is still uncertain.
conditions.why: It mimics a neoplasm clinically and on imaging, and a preoperative biopsy was consistently non-diagnostic before complete resection in one series, so the diagnosis rests on MRI and the resected specimen; the most diagnostic finding was a shell of T2 hypointensity around each lobule. Endoscopic removal was complete in all 25 patients of one series (13 by endoscopic medial maxillectomy and 12 by endoscopic sinus surgery) with no major complications or recurrence, and in a 20-patient series sublabial and endonasal endoscopic approaches, alone or combined, gave no recurrence. The lesion contains neovascularization and frond-like enhancing arteries have been shown on contrast CT in five patients.

imaging.ct: In 12 patients (Kim) the lesion was a unilateral mass of 2.2 to 6.0 cm (mean 4.2), expansile in nine, centred in the maxillary sinus in 11 and the nasal cavity in 1; the ipsilateral nasal cavity was involved in 9 of 11 maxillary lesions and smooth sinus wall erosion other than of the medial wall was seen in 8. In 8 patients, all lesions were hyperdense on precontrast CT, all had smooth erosion of the medial maxillary wall, and the epicentre was the secondary maxillary ostium (Hur). Other series describe heterogeneous enhancement, bony destruction in 25% and focal calcification in 15% of 20 patients (Song), and geographic bone remodeling with thinning of turbinates and sinus walls (Eissa). One series concluded that CT does not help to separate these lesions from neoplasm (Wu).
imaging.mri: T2: marked heterogeneous hypointensity and isointensity with a hypointense peripheral rim, and marked irregular nodular, papillary or frond-like enhancement in all 10 patients imaged (Kim); the hypointense shells correspond to rims of fibrosis around lobules with fresh hemorrhage at the centre (Wu). Unrestricted diffusion with high ADC in the five patients examined (Eissa).

redFlags: Unilateral expansile maxillary mass with epistaxis, smooth wall erosion, hyperdensity on non-contrast CT and a T2-hypointense rim → organized hematoma belongs in the differential before assuming malignancy; a nondiagnostic biopsy is typical.
Associated vascular lesions → 2 of 7 patients in one series had a vascular malformation or small hemangioma next to the mass on final pathology.

pearls.text: The bone changes are described differently between series: smooth erosion in a 12-patient and an 8-patient CT series (medial maxillary wall in all 8 of the latter) against bony destruction in 25% of 20 patients in a third.
Presentation: nasal bleeding in 14 of 25 (Jeong), epistaxis as the most common complaint in 70% of 20 (Song), and epistaxis as the primary complaint in 3 of 7 (Wu).

conditions.name: Nasal bone and septal fracture
conditions.what: Fracture of the nasal bones from blunt facial trauma, often with a fracture or deviation of the septum. It is a common injury and is often managed initially with closed reduction of the nasal bones.
conditions.why: The septum decides the result. After closed nasal reduction without septal reduction, over 90% of patients were satisfied overall, but those with a septal fracture on CT reported worse breathing outcomes (53.6% against 24.1% disagreed that reduction improved nasal breathing) and a septal fracture on imaging was a significant risk factor for later septorhinoplasty (11 patients, 2%, eventually had one). The authors advise counselling about the high risk of persistent deformity and obstruction and addressing a septal fracture early by closed septal reduction or early aggressive management. In 116 patients with isolated nasal bone fractures closed reduction reduced the extent of later septal deviation, so a patient who declines reduction should be told the likely outcome.

imaging.ct: A septal fracture seen on CT is the finding that predicted both the choice of closed reduction and a worse result after it. Septal deviation was measured on coronal CT as the angle between the most prominent point of the septum and the crista galli (the method used in the 116-patient series).

redFlags: Septal fracture on CT → counsel on the high risk of posttraumatic deformity and obstruction despite closed reduction of the nasal bones.
Septal swelling or obstruction after nasal trauma → septal hematoma until proved otherwise ([[dz.septal-hematoma-abscess]]); it is easily missed.

conditions.name: Medial orbital wall (lamina papyracea) fracture
conditions.what: A fracture of the thin medial wall of the orbit, from blunt orbital trauma, that may occur alone or with the orbital floor ([[dz.orbital-floor-fracture]]). Orbital content can prolapse into the ethmoid labyrinth.
conditions.why: Most isolated fractures need no operation: of 60 patients 51 (85%) had no symptoms, 9 (15%) had diplopia, and 56 were managed conservatively, with surgery in 4 for persistent diplopia with enophthalmos. When repair is needed, endoscopic repair with mesh pushed into the orbit was not inferior to the transcaruncular route and took less time (44.7 against 73.9 minutes; 26 endoscopic and 14 external repairs), and diplopia, eye-movement limitation and enophthalmos resolved in all patients except one with preexisting strabismus. For the sinus surgeon the fracture also changes the ethmoid: in a 21-case CT study the plane through the pars membranacea was the most severely affected, and two late fronto-ethmoidal mucoceles appeared 23 and 14 years after the trauma ([[dz.mucocele]]).

imaging.ct: Coronal CT shows the extent of the medial wall defect, the volume of orbital content prolapsed into the ethmoid, and soft-tissue density around the prolapsed content; in 21 cases the coronal plane containing the pars membranacea was the most severely damaged, followed by the plane of the superior meatus. Three-dimensional CT confirmed the fracture location in a 60-patient series, and defect size on preoperative CT was compared between repair routes in 40 patients.

redFlags: Persistent diplopia (more than 2 weeks) with enophthalmos → surgical repair; this applied to 4 of the 60 patients in the series.
Old medial orbital trauma with proptosis, orbital or frontal swelling → late fronto-ethmoidal mucocele, reported in 2 of 21 patients in one series.

conditions.name: Zygomaticomaxillary complex (tripod) fracture
conditions.what: A fracture of the cheek bone (zygoma) at its articulations, one of the most commonly treated facial fractures. Because it alters orbital volume, accurate reduction matters for more than appearance.
conditions.why: Three points matter to a sinus and skull-base surgeon. The infraorbital nerve is injured in about half of patients (pooled incidence 51.9%, 95% CI 48-55%, from 11 trials and 802 patients), and surgical decompression within two weeks gave better sensory recovery than conservative treatment. Accurate reduction and fixation of the zygoma, with internal orbital reconstruction where needed, protects against functional sequelae from orbital volume change. And the maxillary sinus can be affected years later: maxillary mucocele is a late complication of facial fractures even when the ostium is normal (two cases), and in one patient a mucosa-lined closed cavity formed when an untreated orbital floor fracture contacted the anteriorly displaced posterior maxillary wall and produced a cyst 28 years after repair, drained by a combined subciliary and endoscopic endonasal approach.

imaging.ct: CT confirms the fracture (radiologically confirmed fractures defined the meta-analysis population) and allows a strut-based classification of facial fractures in which zygomatic (tripod) and zygomaticomaxillary fractures are complex strut fractures. Look at the orbital floor and the posterior maxillary wall: in the late-cyst case CT showed the bony partition and a posteriorly expanding cyst with bone erosion abutting the orbital contents.

redFlags: Cheek pain or swelling, proptosis or globe displacement years after a facial fracture → late maxillary sinus mucocele or cyst; image with CT (two reported cases of post-traumatic maxillary mucocele with proptosis and globe displacement).
Infraorbital numbness after ZMC fracture → the pooled incidence is about half; early decompression within two weeks was associated with better recovery.

conditions.name: Septal perforation or absent septum
conditions.what: A full-thickness defect through the nasal septum, from a small hole to near or total absence of the septum. This entity is the established finding; the surgical hazard of creating one is [[h.septal-perforation]].
conditions.why: The septum is the midline reference for the whole nasal cavity, so a perforation changes the operation: the septum cannot be assumed present or centred, a nasoseptal flap pedicle or donor mucosa may be unusable on that side, and a defect must be known before it is enlarged. On a specimen it also means the left and right airways communicate.

imaging.ct: A full-thickness defect in the septum on CT; the imaging series read measured its size in two dimensions.

pearls.text: In a CT review of 3,708 consecutive facial-bone CT patients at one urban hospital, 2.05% had a septal perforation. This is a hospital imaging population, not a general-population estimate; the abstract read gives no definition and no location breakdown.

classifications.name: Inflammatory sinonasal disease patterns on CT (Babbel–Harnsberger)
classifications.basis: Distribution of inflammatory mucosal disease on screening coronal CT, grouped by the drainage pathway that is blocked (Babbel et al. 1992, building on the ostiomeatal unit concept of Zinreich and Kennedy).

classes.label: Infundibular pattern
classes.criterion: Disease limited to the maxillary sinus, with obstruction of the ethmoidal infundibulum or maxillary ostium.
classes.why: Uncinectomy and a maxillary antrostomy that includes the natural ostium.

classes.label: Ostiomeatal unit pattern
classes.criterion: Obstruction in the middle meatus with ipsilateral maxillary, anterior ethmoid and frontal disease; the frontal sinus may be spared when it drains medial to the uncinate (lamina papyracea insertion).
classes.why: Uncinectomy, antrostomy and anterior ethmoidectomy, with frontal recess surgery when the frontal sinus is involved.

classes.label: Sphenoethmoidal recess pattern
classes.criterion: Posterior ethmoid and sphenoid disease from obstruction of the sphenoethmoidal recess.
classes.why: Sphenoidotomy ± posterior ethmoidectomy; the anterior sinuses may be left alone.

classes.label: Sinonasal polyposis pattern
classes.criterion: Diffuse polypoid disease of the nasal cavity and sinuses: bilateral pan-opacification, widened infundibula, convex (bulging) ethmoid walls, thinned septa.
classes.why: Diffuse disease: complete surgery plus long-term medical or biologic therapy, not targeted drainage.

classes.label: Sporadic (unclassifiable) pattern
classes.criterion: Isolated disease not explained by an obstructed pathway — retention cysts, mucoceles, isolated mucosal thickening, postoperative change.
classes.why: Usually not an indication for drainage surgery by itself; consider a local cause.

classifications.caveats: Descriptive rather than a stage: patterns overlap in one patient, and frontal recess cell anatomy (IFAC) is not captured. Its value is the first question when reading any CT — which drainage pathway is blocked, and does the disease fit it? Disease that fits no pathway (unilateral, expansile, hyperdense) needs another explanation.

classifications.name: Lund–Mackay CT score
classifications.basis: CT opacification of each sinus group and the ostiomeatal complex, scored per side (Lund & Mackay 1993); used for chronic rhinosinusitis with or without polyps.

classes.label: Clear
classes.criterion: No opacification of the sinus; for the ostiomeatal complex, not occluded.

classes.label: Partial opacification
classes.criterion: Partial opacification of the maxillary, anterior ethmoid, posterior ethmoid, sphenoid or frontal sinus (the ostiomeatal complex has no score of 1).

classes.label: Complete opacification
classes.criterion: Complete opacification of the sinus, or an occluded ostiomeatal complex.

classes.label: Total score
classes.criterion: Five sinus groups (0–2 each) plus the ostiomeatal complex (0 or 2): 0–12 per side, 0–24 in total.
classes.why: An objective CT benchmark for staging, trials and consensus criteria; it correlates weakly with symptoms.

classifications.caveats: People without CRS commonly score a few points — the mean was about 4 of 24 in one CT series of adults scanned for non-sinus reasons — so a low score neither proves nor excludes CRS. It ignores osteitis, hyperdense contents and frontal recess anatomy, and scans taken during an acute episode overstate it.

classifications.name: Lund–Kennedy endoscopic score
classifications.basis: Endoscopic appearance of each side scored 0–2 for five features (Lund & Kennedy); the modified score (Psaltis et al. 2014) keeps polyps, discharge and edema only.

classes.label: Polyps
classes.criterion: 0 absent; 1 confined to the middle meatus; 2 beyond the middle meatus.

classes.label: Discharge
classes.criterion: 0 none; 1 clear and thin; 2 thick and purulent.

classes.label: Edema
classes.criterion: 0 absent; 1 mild; 2 severe.

classes.label: Scarring (postoperative)
classes.criterion: 0 absent; 1 mild; 2 severe.

classes.label: Crusting (postoperative)
classes.criterion: 0 absent; 1 mild; 2 severe.

classes.label: Total
classes.criterion: Original: 0–10 per side, 0–20 in total. Modified Lund–Kennedy (polyps, discharge, edema): 0–6 per side, 0–12 in total.
classes.why: The modified score is more reliable and tracks patient-reported outcomes better; use it to follow the postoperative cavity.

classifications.caveats: Scarring and crusting reflect surgery and healing more than disease activity. The polyp item is coarse; biologic trials use the 0–4 per side polyp score ([[c.nasal-polyp-score]]).

classifications.name: Nasal polyp score (0–4 per side)
classifications.basis: Endoscopic polyp extent graded 0–4 on each side and summed (0–8); the primary endoscopic endpoint of phase 3 biologic trials in CRSwNP.

classes.label: None
classes.criterion: No polyps.

classes.label: Middle meatus
classes.criterion: Small polyps in the middle meatus not reaching below the inferior border of the middle turbinate.

classes.label: Below the middle turbinate
classes.criterion: Polyps reaching below the lower border of the middle turbinate.

classes.label: Large
classes.criterion: Large polyps reaching the lower border of the inferior turbinate, or polyps medial to the middle turbinate.

classes.label: Obstructing
classes.criterion: Large polyps causing complete obstruction of the inferior nasal cavity.

classifications.caveats: Several polyp grading systems exist (Meltzer, Lildholdt, the Lund–Kennedy polyp item) and they are not interchangeable; check which one a trial or an eligibility rule uses.

classifications.name: EPOS 2020 classification of chronic rhinosinusitis
classifications.basis: Primary versus secondary CRS; then anatomic distribution (localized, usually unilateral, versus diffuse, bilateral); then endotype dominance (type 2 or non-type 2) for primary disease, or cause for secondary disease (EPOS 2020).

classes.label: Primary, localized, type 2
classes.criterion: Unilateral type 2 disease: allergic fungal rhinosinusitis.
classes.why: [[dz.afrs]]

classes.label: Primary, localized, non-type 2
classes.criterion: Isolated sinusitis of one sinus without another cause.

classes.label: Primary, diffuse, type 2
classes.criterion: Bilateral type 2 disease: eosinophilic CRS (usually with polyps; tissue eosinophils ≥10/hpf), bilateral AFRS, central compartment atopic disease.
classes.why: Complete surgery, corticosteroids and, when criteria are met, biologics ([[dz.crs-with-polyps]], [[dz.aerd]], [[dz.ccad]]).

classes.label: Primary, diffuse, non-type 2
classes.criterion: Bilateral non-eosinophilic CRS (tissue eosinophils below the threshold).
classes.why: Often without polyps; targeted surgery and anti-inflammatory therapy ([[dz.crs-without-polyps]]).

classes.label: Secondary, localized
classes.criterion: Local pathology: odontogenic disease, fungal ball, tumor.
classes.why: Treat the cause ([[dz.odontogenic-sinusitis]], [[dz.fungal-ball]]).

classes.label: Secondary, diffuse
classes.criterion: Mechanical (primary ciliary dyskinesia, cystic fibrosis), inflammatory (GPA, EGPA) or immunological (immunodeficiency).
classes.why: Systemic workup and disease-specific treatment ([[dz.cystic-fibrosis-sinusitis]], [[dz.gpa]]).

classifications.caveats: Endotype is inferred in practice from surrogates — tissue or blood eosinophils, total IgE, asthma — and eosinophil thresholds vary between populations. The CRSwNP/CRSsNP phenotype split remains in use alongside this scheme.

classifications.name: Bent–Kuhn criteria for allergic fungal rhinosinusitis
classifications.basis: Five major criteria, all required for the diagnosis, with minor criteria that support it (Bent & Kuhn 1994).

classes.label: Type I hypersensitivity
classes.criterion: IgE-mediated hypersensitivity to fungi by history, skin test or specific IgE.

classes.label: Nasal polyposis
classes.criterion: Polyps on endoscopy or imaging.

classes.label: Characteristic CT
classes.criterion: Heterogeneous hyperdense contents in expanded, opacified sinuses, often with bone remodeling or erosion.

classes.label: Eosinophilic mucin without invasion
classes.criterion: Eosinophil-rich mucin and no fungal invasion of sinus tissue on histology (Charcot–Leyden crystals are a minor criterion).

classes.label: Positive fungal stain
classes.criterion: Fungal hyphae in the mucin on stain; culture may be negative.

classes.label: Minor criteria
classes.criterion: Asthma, unilateral predominance, radiographic bone erosion, positive fungal culture, Charcot–Leyden crystals, peripheral eosinophilia.

classifications.caveats: Eosinophilic mucin CRS without demonstrable fungi looks the same, and how essential fungal allergy is remains debated. Culture is neither sensitive nor specific — stain the mucin. Bone erosion is common but only a minor criterion.

classifications.name: Classification of fungal rhinosinusitis
classifications.basis: Tissue invasion on histology (invasive versus non-invasive), then host immunity, time course and host response (deShazo et al. 1997).

classes.label: Acute (fulminant) invasive
classes.criterion: Hyphae invading mucosa, submucosa, vessels or bone; course under 4 weeks; immunocompromised host.
classes.why: Surgical emergency: debridement, antifungals and reversal of immunosuppression ([[dz.acute-invasive-fungal-sinusitis]]).

classes.label: Chronic invasive
classes.criterion: Tissue invasion with a course over 12 weeks and sparse inflammation; often diabetic or mildly immunocompromised host.
classes.why: Debridement and a prolonged antifungal course ([[dz.chronic-invasive-fungal-sinusitis]]).

classes.label: Granulomatous invasive
classes.criterion: Tissue invasion with non-caseating granulomas, usually Aspergillus flavus in immunocompetent hosts; chronic course.
classes.why: Debridement and antifungals; often presents as a cheek or orbital mass.

classes.label: Fungal ball (non-invasive)
classes.criterion: Dense hyphae in one sinus; no invasion, no allergic mucin.
classes.why: Endoscopic removal alone ([[dz.fungal-ball]]).

classes.label: Allergic fungal rhinosinusitis (non-invasive)
classes.criterion: Eosinophilic mucin with hyphae, type I hypersensitivity and polyps; no invasion.
classes.why: Surgery plus steroids ([[dz.afrs]]).

classes.label: Saprophytic fungal colonization
classes.criterion: Fungi growing on crusts in an operated cavity, without invasion.
classes.why: Endoscopic removal of crusts.

classifications.caveats: The dividing line is invasion of tissue on histology, so every debridement of suspected fungal disease sends tissue, not only secretions. The 4- and 12-week limits are conventions, and forms can convert — a fungal ball in a newly immunosuppressed patient can become invasive.

classifications.name: Frontal sinus fracture pattern
classifications.basis: Which walls are fractured and how displaced, plus frontal sinus outflow tract and dural involvement — the elements that management algorithms use (e.g. Rodriguez et al. 2008); there is no single universally adopted numbered system.

classes.label: Anterior table, non-displaced
classes.criterion: Anterior table fracture without contour deformity; posterior table and outflow tract intact.
classes.why: Observe.

classes.label: Anterior table, displaced
classes.criterion: Displaced or comminuted anterior table with contour deformity; posterior table intact.
classes.why: Reduce and fix for contour (open or endoscope-assisted), or camouflage later.

classes.label: Outflow tract involved
classes.criterion: Fracture through the sinus floor, medial orbital roof or anterior ethmoid at the frontal recess, or fragments obstructing it.
classes.why: Mucocele and chronic sinusitis risk: CT follow-up and endoscopic frontal sinusotomy (Draf IIa–III) if drainage fails; obliteration is now a secondary option.

classes.label: Posterior table, non-displaced
classes.criterion: Posterior table fracture without significant displacement and without a persistent CSF leak.
classes.why: Observe; conservative care of any transient leak.

classes.label: Posterior table, displaced or comminuted
classes.criterion: Displaced or comminuted posterior table, often with dural tear, persistent CSF leak, pneumocephalus or brain injury.
classes.why: Neurosurgical repair; cranialization for severe comminution.

classifications.caveats: Patterns combine (e.g. AT-D with OT). Thresholds for "significant" displacement differ between algorithms; a persistent CSF leak and the state of the outflow tract drive decisions more than millimetres do.

classifications.name: Markowitz–Manson classification of naso-orbito-ethmoid fractures
classifications.basis: State of the central bone fragment that carries the medial canthal tendon (Markowitz et al. 1991).

classes.label: Type I
classes.criterion: A single large central fragment with the medial canthal tendon attached (unilateral or bilateral, complete or incomplete).
classes.why: Plate the fragment; the tendon follows it.

classes.label: Type II
classes.criterion: Comminuted central fragment, but the tendon remains attached to a fragment large enough to fix.
classes.why: Fix the tendon-bearing fragment, often with transnasal wiring.

classes.label: Type III
classes.criterion: Severe comminution with the tendon avulsed or attached to fragments too small to fix.
classes.why: Transnasal canthopexy plus bone grafting of the medial orbital wall and nasal dorsum.

classifications.caveats: Final typing is often made at surgery, by exposing the fragment and testing the tendon; CT suggests the type but can underestimate comminution.

classifications.name: Curaçao criteria for hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia
classifications.basis: Four clinical criteria; the number met gives definite, possible or unlikely HHT (Shovlin et al. 2000). Genetic testing can confirm.

classes.label: Epistaxis
classes.criterion: Spontaneous, recurrent nosebleeds.

classes.label: Telangiectases
classes.criterion: Multiple, at characteristic sites: lips, oral cavity, fingers, nose.

classes.label: Visceral lesions
classes.criterion: Gastrointestinal telangiectasia, or pulmonary, hepatic, cerebral or spinal arteriovenous malformations.

classes.label: Family history
classes.criterion: A first-degree relative with HHT by these criteria.

classes.label: Definite HHT
classes.criterion: Three or four criteria.

classes.label: Possible or suspected HHT
classes.criterion: Two criteria.

classes.label: Unlikely HHT
classes.criterion: Fewer than two criteria.

classifications.caveats: Children and young adults may not yet meet the criteria because lesions accumulate with age; in families with a known mutation, genetic testing settles the diagnosis.

classifications.name: 2022 ACR/EULAR classification criteria for granulomatosis with polyangiitis
classifications.basis: Weighted clinical, laboratory, imaging and biopsy items, summed only after a small- or medium-vessel vasculitis has been diagnosed and mimics excluded; a total of 5 or more classifies as GPA (Robson et al. 2022).

classes.label: Nasal involvement (+3)
classes.criterion: Bloody discharge, ulcers, crusting, congestion or blockage, or septal defect or perforation.

classes.label: Cartilaginous involvement (+2)
classes.criterion: Ear or nose cartilage inflammation, hoarse voice or stridor, endobronchial involvement, or saddle nose deformity.

classes.label: Hearing loss (+1)
classes.criterion: Conductive or sensorineural hearing loss.

classes.label: cANCA or anti-PR3 positive (+5)
classes.criterion: Positive test for cytoplasmic ANCA or anti-proteinase 3 antibodies.

classes.label: Lung nodules, mass or cavitation (+2)
classes.criterion: On chest imaging.

classes.label: Granuloma on biopsy (+2)
classes.criterion: Granuloma, extravascular granulomatous inflammation or giant cells on biopsy.

classes.label: Sinonasal inflammation on imaging (+1)
classes.criterion: Inflammation, consolidation or effusion of the nasal or paranasal sinuses, or mastoiditis, on imaging.

classes.label: Pauci-immune glomerulonephritis (+1)
classes.criterion: On biopsy.

classes.label: pANCA or anti-MPO positive (−1)
classes.criterion: Positive test for perinuclear ANCA or anti-myeloperoxidase antibodies.

classes.label: Blood eosinophils ≥1 × 10⁹/L (−4)
classes.criterion: Peripheral eosinophil count at or above 1 × 10⁹/L.

classes.label: Classified as GPA
classes.criterion: Total score ≥5.

classifications.caveats: These are classification criteria for studies, not diagnostic criteria: apply them only after a vasculitis is diagnosed and mimics — cocaine-induced lesions, lymphoma, infection — are excluded. Nasal items weigh heavily, so a crusting nose with PR3-ANCA reaches the threshold by itself, which is exactly the cocaine trap.

classifications.name: Revised diagnostic criteria for pseudotumor cerebri (Friedman)
classifications.basis: Papilledema-based diagnosis with a normal neurological examination, imaging and CSF composition and a raised opening pressure, plus defined routes to diagnosis without papilledema (Friedman et al. 2013).

classes.label: Papilledema
classes.criterion: Papilledema present.

classes.label: Normal neurological examination
classes.criterion: Normal apart from cranial nerve abnormalities.

classes.label: Neuroimaging
classes.criterion: Normal brain parenchyma without hydrocephalus, mass, structural lesion or abnormal meningeal enhancement on MRI with and without gadolinium; MR venography as well in atypical patients (anyone other than obese women), to exclude venous sinus thrombosis.

classes.label: CSF composition
classes.criterion: Normal CSF composition.

classes.label: Opening pressure
classes.criterion: Lumbar puncture opening pressure ≥250 mm CSF in adults, ≥280 mm CSF in children (≥250 mm if the child is neither sedated nor obese).

classes.label: Definite
classes.criterion: A–E all met.

classes.label: Probable
classes.criterion: A–D met with a lower opening pressure.

classes.label: Without papilledema
classes.criterion: B–E plus a unilateral or bilateral abducens palsy makes the diagnosis; without an abducens palsy, B–E plus at least three of four imaging signs — empty sella, flattened posterior globe, distended perioptic subarachnoid space ± tortuous optic nerve, transverse venous sinus stenosis — only suggests it.

classifications.caveats: In spontaneous CSF leaks the leak vents the pressure, so papilledema and opening pressure may be normal until the leak is closed; before repair, the imaging signs carry the most weight.

classifications.name: 2022 ACR/EULAR classification criteria for eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis
classifications.basis: Seven weighted items, summed only after a small- or medium-vessel vasculitis has been diagnosed and mimics of vasculitis excluded; a cumulative score of 6 or more classifies as EGPA (Grayson et al. 2022). Developed and validated as classification criteria for research, not as diagnostic criteria.

classes.label: Maximum eosinophil count (+5)
classes.criterion: Maximum blood eosinophil count at or above 1 x 10^9/L.

classes.label: Obstructive airway disease (+3)
classes.criterion: Obstructive airway disease, as named in the published criteria.

classes.label: Nasal polyps (+3)
classes.criterion: Nasal polyps, as named in the published criteria.
classes.why: The only sinonasal item in the criteria; polyps alone score 3 of the 6 points needed, so they cannot classify EGPA without other items.

classes.label: cANCA or anti-PR3 positive (-3)
classes.criterion: Cytoplasmic ANCA or anti-proteinase 3 ANCA positivity; this item subtracts points.

classes.label: Extravascular eosinophilic-predominant inflammation (+2)
classes.criterion: Extravascular eosinophil-predominant inflammation, as named in the published criteria.

classes.label: Mononeuritis multiplex or motor neuropathy (+1)
classes.criterion: Mononeuritis multiplex or motor neuropathy not due to radiculopathy.

classes.label: Hematuria (-1)
classes.criterion: Hematuria; this item subtracts a point.

classifications.caveats: Derived from 107 EGPA cases and 450 comparators and validated in a separate set of 119 cases and 437 comparators: sensitivity 85% (95% CI 77-91%), specificity 99% (95% CI 98-100%). The point values are from the abstract; the exact definition of each item is in the full paper, which this entry has not read, so the criterion wording above only names the items. Eleven items were identified by regression from 91 candidates and seven were retained.

classifications.name: Wise CT bone-remodeling score for allergic fungal rhinosinusitis
classifications.basis: A CT score of how much of the sinus bony walls is expanded or eroded (Wise et al. 2009): each paranasal sinus wall with expansion or erosion scores 1 point, capped per sinus, plus the intersinus septa, for a maximum of 24. It scores bone change, not opacification or mucosal disease.

classes.label: Frontal sinus, each side
classes.criterion: One point per wall with expansion or erosion, maximum 3 points for each frontal sinus.

classes.label: Ethmoid complex, each side
classes.criterion: One point per wall with expansion or erosion, maximum 2 points for each ethmoid complex.

classes.label: Sphenoid sinus, each side
classes.criterion: One point per wall with expansion or erosion, maximum 3 points for each sphenoid sinus.

classes.label: Maxillary sinus, each side
classes.criterion: One point per wall with expansion or erosion, maximum 3 points for each maxillary sinus.

classes.label: Intersinus septa
classes.criterion: One point each for the frontal and the sphenoid intersinus septum, 2 points in all.

classes.label: Total score
classes.criterion: Sum of the components above, 0 to 24.
classes.why: In the 111 scored CT scans the mean was 7.8 (range 0 to 24).

classifications.caveats: Read from the abstract only: which walls count toward each sinus's maximum is not stated there. The abstract reports that males scored higher than females (mean 9.3 vs 5.6) and African American patients higher than Caucasian patients (9.6 vs 5.0) and says outcome prediction was still to be analysed, so it is a descriptive score, not a validated prognostic stage. It does not replace the diagnostic criteria in [[c.bent-kuhn-afrs]]. For follow-up after surgery a separate endoscopic score exists (Philpott-Javer 2011: each of the maxillary, ethmoid, frontal and sphenoid cavities scored 0 to 9 for mucosal oedema plus 1 point for fungal mucin, maximum 40 per side, built to refine the 4-stage (0 to 3) Kupferberg global grade); the individual grades are not given in the abstract and are not reproduced here.

measurements.name: Subperiosteal orbital abscess volume at which drainage is favoured
measurements.what: CT volume of a subperiosteal orbital abscess above which published pediatric series found surgical drainage usually needed. The range runs from the lowest to the highest cut-off reported by the three series read; it is not a population distribution, and each cut-off was derived and measured differently.
measurements.population: Children with a subperiosteal orbital abscess complicating sinusitis (retrospective single-centre series).
measurements.note: Where the studies disagree: McCoy 2021 (108 children) took a receiver-operating-characteristic cut-off of 0.510 cm3 (510 mm3; sensitivity 71.2%, specificity 84.4%) and, using 0.500 cm3, found 42 of 49 (85.7%) abscesses at or above it were drained against 17 of 55 (30.9%) below it; its volume is the product of the three CT dimensions, not an ellipsoid, and a 1 cm3 reference left 41% of the smaller abscesses needing surgery. Tabarino 2015 (32 children with abscess, spheroid-model volume) reported that all patients with a volume above 500 mm3 (or above 5% of orbital volume) were operated on, against 30% (39%) of those with smaller volumes. Todman 2011 (29 patients, volume from the largest axial, coronal and sagittal dimensions) reported that volumes below 1,250 mm3 did not require surgery, and PubMed prints that unit without its superscript. Part of the gap is how volume was computed and what the cut-off means (an ROC optimum, a level above which all were drained, a level below which none were); the abstracts do not show that this accounts for all of it, and the series are small and retrospective. A review (Appachi 2020) states there is consensus that large-volume abscesses need drainage but that the cut-off differs between studies; a meta-analysis (Adil 2020) pooled a risk ratio of 3.61 for surgery above each study's own threshold. Ryan 2009 reported surgical patients had larger abscesses (>10 mm); its abstract does not say which dimension. McCoy 2021 frames a volume of 0.510 cm3 or larger, in any location, as a relative indication for surgery.
